notes.meaning: Matthew opens his Gospel by presenting the family line of Jesus Christ. He identifies Jesus as both the son of David and the son of Abraham. This proves that Jesus inherits the royal kingdom promised to David and brings the worldwide blessing promised to Abraham.

The family record begins with Abraham and traces through Isaac and Jacob down to Judah and his brothers. God chose Isaac over Ishmael, and Jacob over Esau, displaying his divine choice in carrying forward the promise. Judah is named because the royal ruler would come from his tribe, but his brothers are included because all twelve tribes share in God's covenant family.

The family line continues from Judah to Perez and Zerah through Tamar, and continues down to Salmon. Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law, and her mention recalls a painful family history that displays God's grace to fallen humanity. The list also includes Ram and Amminadab, leading to Nahshon, who served as a leader in the tribe of Judah during Israel's journey through the wilderness.

Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse, the father of King David. Rahab and Ruth were both Gentiles, which reveals that God's plan of salvation was open to outsiders from the very start. David is specifically called 'the king' because God established the royal line with him, though the mention of Uriah's wife reminds readers of human weakness and divine forgiveness.

The royal line continues from Solomon through the kings of Judah down to Uzziah. Matthew leaves out three kings between Joram and Uzziah—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—which was a standard practice in Jewish genealogical lists. This succession of rulers contained both faithful and ungodly kings, showing that God's grace is not passed down by physical inheritance.

The family line passes from Uzziah through Jotham and Ahaz to the faithful king Hezekiah, followed by Manasseh, Amon, and Josiah. This era of Judah's history was marked by deep spiritual trials and the rising threat of foreign empires. Even during times of widespread idolatry, the Lord remained faithful to his covenant to preserve David's royal line.

Josiah's royal line brings the history down to Jeconiah during the painful era when the Jewish people were forced into exile in Babylon. Even though Judah lost its earthly independence and the throne was cast down, God did not let David's line disappear. The royal descent was preserved through the captivity in Shealtiel and Zerubbabel.

Zerubbabel's lineage moves through Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, and Matthan to Jacob. These generations span the quiet period after the return from exile when David's royal family lived in humble obscurity. Although these men were not crowned monarchs, their names were kept in family records until the arrival of the promised Deliverer.

Jacob fathered Joseph, who is introduced not as the physical father of Jesus, but as the husband of Mary. By marrying Mary, Joseph provided Jesus with the legal right to David's royal throne under Jewish law. The name 'Christ' means the Anointed One, identifying Jesus as the true Prophet, Priest, and King promised to Israel.

differ.view: Luke records Mary's actual physical descent, while Matthew provides Joseph's legal royal line.
Both Matthew and Luke trace Joseph's ancestry, using distinct legal and family tables.

notes.meaning: Matthew arranges the long line of ancestors into three groups of fourteen generations, centered on Abraham, David, and the Babylonian exile. This pattern served as an easy aid to memory and reflected three major stages in Israel's national life. The arrangement demonstrates that God steered human history across many centuries toward the coming of Christ.

Matthew explains that Mary was betrothed, or pledged in marriage, to Joseph. In Jewish practice, betrothal was a binding legal agreement that required a formal divorce to break, even though the couple did not yet share a home or live as husband and wife. Before their marriage was completed, Mary was found to be pregnant through the miraculous power of the Holy Spirit rather than any human father.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view Matthew's birth story as creative Jewish storytelling rather than historical fact.

notes.meaning: Joseph was an upright man who loved God's law, yet he had no desire to subject Mary to public shame or the law's harshest penalties. Unfaithfulness during betrothal was considered adultery, which could be punished with public trial and execution. To avoid humiliating her, Joseph planned to end the agreement quietly by delivering a private divorce document before only two or three witnesses.

While Joseph was wrestling with this painful choice, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The angel addressed him as 'son of David' to remind him of his royal heritage and God's ancient promises. Joseph was instructed not to fear completing the marriage, because the child in Mary was conceived by the direct work of the Holy Spirit.

The angel announced that Mary would bear a son, and Joseph was instructed to name him Jesus. The name Jesus means 'the Lord saves,' which pointed directly to his divine mission. He came not merely to deliver his people from earthly oppressors, but to free them from the penalty and power of their sins.

These events fulfilled the ancient prophecy from Isaiah that a virgin would conceive and give birth to a son. Matthew explains that the child would be called Immanuel, which translates to 'God with us.' Jesus is truly God united with human nature, entering the world to dwell among us and reconcile us to the Father.

When Joseph woke from his sleep, he put aside his previous doubts and immediately obeyed the angel's instruction. He took Mary into his home as his lawful wife, gladly shielding her honor and embracing his role in God's plan. His quick and willing response demonstrated genuine faith and submission to the Lord.

Joseph refrained from marital relations with Mary until she brought forth her firstborn son, ensuring that the miraculous nature of the virgin birth remained beyond dispute. In obedience to the angel's command, Joseph gave the child the name Jesus at his circumcision. By naming the child, Joseph acted as his legal earthly father and formally registered him into David's royal lineage.

differ.view: The word 'until' does not imply that Mary had other children later, and early Reformers affirmed her lifelong virginity.
Mary's virginity prior to Christ's birth is essential to Christian faith, but her lifelong virginity cannot be proven from the text.
The text only addresses the period up to the birth of Jesus, leaving later marital life unstated, so speculation should be avoided.
The natural sense of the language suggests that Joseph and Mary shared normal marital relations and had other children after Jesus was born.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary remained a virgin throughout her entire life, as 'until' does not denote later marital relations, and Jesus' brothers were close relatives.
